statement: A board has 4 rows and 7 columns of squares. One square is removed, and the remaining 27 squares are to be covered exactly by nine 1 by 3 tiles, each lying along a row or down a column. How many of the 28 squares could be the removed one?

choices.misconception: I checked that removing a corner works and assumed that only the four corners could be removed.
I used one diagonal colouring with three colours and counted the 10 squares of the colour that appears most, without also using the colouring along the other diagonals.
I used a chessboard colouring and thought the removed square must be black, but a 1 by 3 tile does not cover one square of each of two colours.
I only checked that 27 is a multiple of 3, so I thought any square could be removed.

hints: Colour along diagonals with three colours, so every tile covers each colour once.
Give the square in row r, column c the colour (r + c) mod 3. Each tile covers every colour once, so the removed square has the colour with one extra square. Repeat with (r - c) mod 3.
Numbering rows 1 to 4 and columns 1 to 7, both colourings single out the squares in rows 1 and 4 and columns 1, 4 and 7. Check that each of these really works.

solutions.reliable: Colour the square in row r and column c with colour (r + c) mod 3. A 1 by 3 tile, across or down, always covers one square of each colour. The board has 10 squares of one colour (the colour of the top-left corner) and 9 of each of the others, so for the 27 remaining squares to split 9, 9, 9 the removed square must have that colour. The same argument with colour (r - c) mod 3 gives a second condition. With rows numbered 1 to 4 and columns 1 to 7, the squares passing both tests are those in rows 1 and 4 and columns 1, 4 and 7: six squares. Each of them works: if the removed square is in the top row, the rest of that row splits into pieces of length 3, and the 3 by 7 block below is filled by seven upright tiles; the bottom row is the same upside down. So the answer is 6. The transferable idea: colour so that every tile covers each colour equally; the missing square must then come from the colour in surplus, and two different colourings can be combined.

whyOnTest: Tiling questions with 1 by 3 tiles are settled by a three-colouring along diagonals, and using both diagonal directions is what cuts 10 candidates down to 6.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
